of rheumatism. Miss Smith was
transferred to Rupert from this point
and of late has suffered severely with
rheumatism.

couple of weeks ago. Her daughter

that place.

Cone and Lloyd Leach of the Whit

glass to help us get the far vision and
grow upon the lessons of life.-Grit.

WASHINGTON, March 1.—The attempt of vessel owners to weaken the La Toilette seamen's law was resisted by representatives of seafaring unions before a congressional committee that is considering the Rowe bill. The training period of an able seaman is now three years, and 56 per cent. of the crew must be able seamen. WASHINGTON, June 1—Attorney General Palmer, replying today before the house rules committee, to criticisms leveled at his department by Louis R. Post, assistant secretary of labor, declared Mr. Post had set himself above congress and the law in the handling of deportation cases.

The attorney general asserted that Assistant Secretary Post's entire official career had been marked by a friendliness toward radicals which had done much toward encouraging the growth and development of their program. He further charged that Mr. Post had proceeded on his personal view that the deportation law is wrong and had defied the rules of evidence as laid down by the courts.

Mr. Palmer was before the committee, which is inquiring into the official conduct of Mr. Post, nearly five hours and then did not complete his statement. He urged the committee to delve deep in Mr. Post's record declaring that many things which might interest you could be found.

Citing instances of what he characterized as Mr. Post's maladministration, the attorney general said the assistant labor secretary had seen fit to create in Detroit a committee known as the advisory committee of Detroit citizens which, he said, had been permitted to pass upon all questions of bonds for aliens arrested on deportation warrants.

Mr. Palmer presented to the committee copy of the message to P. L. Prentiss, immigration inspector at Detroit, in which Mr. Post instructed the inspector to release 10 persons on bail of $500. The telegram added that should the advisory committee so elect, the aliens may be paroled in lieu of bail to the committee or such members thereof as the committee may designate.

The department of justice, Mr. Palmer said, had been handicapped for many months because it had coincided with the stubborn incapacity of Louis R. Post, in attempting to round up and rid the country of radicals.

TOPEKA, Kans., March 27.—Especially.
Half the Kansas delegation to the Republican national convention at Chicago has been elected and not one Wood man has been named. In the three districts left there are only two candidates for delegate with pronounced tendencies. Only one of the leading candidates for delegates at large is an active supporter of Wood. None of the ten delegates, so far named, is instructed. Two are pledged not to vote for Wood unless the entire delegation is supporting him. The eighth district convention went on record as opposed to military training and opposed to the nomination of military man.

"President Makers Turned Down."
In the four district conventions held this week the turning down of two leading Kansas president makers were features. In the third Judge Clyde N. Reed of Parsons, who is conducting an active campaign with William Allen White of Emporia, to name Gov. Henry J. Allen for the presidency, went to the convention in person to see that Hugh Powell of Coffeyville and Simo Cossard of Oswego were named delegates. His men both lost; Wilbur Allen of Chanute and Charles N. Hunt of Arkansas City were elected.

"Harder Blow in Eighth District."
The eighth district convention at Newton dealt an even harder blow to Fred Stanley of Wichita, national committeeman from Kansas. Stanley has been issuing statements that Kansas republicans would send Wood delegation to the national convention. Stanley lives in the eighth district, and came from Chicago to attend the convention. He attempted to get a resolution adopted indorsing Gen. Wood for President. The convention not only refused, but adopted one opposing the nomination of any military man.

No attempt to obtain even indorsement for any candidate at the state convention at Salina March 31 is expected, to say nothing of instructions.

"Delegates at Large."
Of the leading candidates for delegate at large, only W. William Watson of Salina is counted Wood supporter. D. W. Mulvane of Topeka, former national committeeman, is understood to prefer either Senator Harding or Gov. Lowden to Wood, although not publicly committed to either.

Willis J. Bailey of Atchison and H. H. Motter of Olathe, while not unfriendly to Wood, are not strongly for him. Emerson Carey of Hutchinson is opposed to Wood, and neither of the two woman candidates for delegate at large, Mrs. R. R. Bittman of Independence and Mrs. Minnie J. Grimstead of Liberal, is favorably inclined toward the Wood candidacy.

CLIFF STRATTON

The second meeting of the Wholesale
merchants of Wilmington yesterday
afternoon, in the Chamber of Commerce
council room, Du Pont Building, resulted
in the organization of Wholesale Section,
to be affiliated with Chamber of
Commerce, and also the election of offi-
cers to serve one year: William
Mullen, representing the W. H. Mullen
Co., was unanimously elected chairman
and the following committee of six was

new unit: W. A. Hapanian, J. A. Booker,

of directors of the Chamber of Com-
merce in January were chosen. They
were John A. Booker, W. H. Mode,
Max Matthews, W. H. Mullen and
Samuel N. J. Dillon.


The advisability of organizing a
section of the Chamber of Commerce or
as an independent body was discussed.
It was pointed out that inasmuch
that Chamber of Commerce would supply the
machinery and aid in every possible
way towards the success of the organis-
ing unit, and because of that fact, it was
unanimously decided that the wholesale
dealers organize and to be affiliated
with the Chamber of Commerce. The
new unit will have the privilege of formu-
lating its own plans closely with others
and the appointment of its own commit-
tees.


Alfred Y. Warner, president of
Chamber of Commerce, in addressing
the wholesale dealers, pointed out the
great need of such an organization and
urged that they become a unit of
Chamber of Commerce. He further stated
that a dealer does not necessarily have
to be a member of Chamber of Commerce
to belong to the organization, and that
they would have the same privileges as
anyone who is a member to mixer
his cooperation in trying to place
Wilmington in the map of trade in the
vicinity.


The organization of the Wholesale
Section is the outcome of reaching nearby
cities, which have
been securing much of the trade, largely
capped by Baltimore and Philadelphia,
the merchants of these two cities have
been taking of the territory and the
shipping trade between Wilmington and
the nearby towns have also become affected.


Truckers have secured nearly all the
shipping trade between the Delaware
towns and the Wholesale merchants of
Baltimore and Philadelphia have taken
advantage of this better mere transportation in the form of motor trucks, and the advantage of the prestige which
larger houses have.


Gamble, traffic superintendent of the
Southern Grand Division of the Louisville
railroad, in a second committee
of the Chamber of Commerce, stated that the weekly
freight service would affect only the
Wilmington and Charleston branches
and that the daily freight service would
be maintained on the main line. Thus
daily service is indeed a big asset to
Wilmington merchants in view of the
heavy shipments which are sent out each
day.


At the next meeting of the section,
which will probably be within the next
two weeks, plans will be considered by
the members and in which it is hoped to
work out method for securing more
trade.

means of sending music by wireless has
been devised by Sergt. Thomas Brass
of the Georgia Tech signal unit, reserve officers training corps. A demon-
stration to the Atlanta Radio club
proved the success of his invention.

Sergt. Brass gave a concert by wire-
less telephone, probably the first in the
history of that device. It was to the
jazzy strains of "Razzle Dazzle" that the
invention was first publicly tested.

soon as complete communication had
been established. Sergt. Brass sent
"Razzle Dazzle" through the instrument
without warning to the listeners. All
were asked to report back what they
heard with the result that the success
of the invention was assured.

ner:

A station in Alabama that is on

made, the pleasure of wireless music
will have to be confined to those who
are fortunate enough to get a headset.

quotations which would attract in
vestors into the far deliveries, and

options would go to carry charges.

ginning of the war that late months
have shown premiums over near po-
sitions; previously values had been
supported by the strength of the
spot situation, but in prewar days
premiums on late months were by
no means unusual. Weekend fig-
ures were bearish, as had been ex-
pected, and trade reports remained
poor.

carried the list off to a net loss of

selling was attracted by the rise,
and the gains were not entirely
maintained. Nervousness over af-
fairs abroad was increased by the

New York, Nov. 5—The stock market was the center of another selling movement today, every branch of the list yielding 2 to 5 per cent on the increasing weight of liquidation at extreme recessions of 2 to 7 points.

There were occasional halts and feeble rallies, but these were succeeded by fresh offerings in which new low levels were registered. The tone of the market at the close was weak on total sales of 1,100,000 shares. Among the stocks that suffered greatest impairment were those comprising the shipping, steel, equipment, oil and motor groups, but even the gilt-edged railway did not escape the general reversal, all save a few of the transcontinentals forfeiting one to three points.

Development over the week-end played into the hands of the shorts, the operations of that fraction adding substantially to the day's unsettlement, especially in the volatile industrials, and securities for which there was a very high demand.

Increased pessimism was engendered by another deficit in clearing house reserves, the lower ratio of reserves reported by the Federal Reserve Bank and tightness of local funds, call loans again rising to 10 per cent after opening at nine per cent.

These conditions were intensified by the further decentralization of foreign exchange and the statement of prominent financier that the country is entering the shadows of a period of industrial depression which may justify corrective legislation.

The break in foreign exchange carried it down to within 2 per cent of its minimum quotation in this market, while French, Italian, Dutch, Spanish and Scandinavian receipts were at lowest levels ever recorded.

Liberty bonds and victory notes reacted moderately and the bond market as a whole was affected by the weakness of stocks, rails, industrials and internationals, closing at variable fractions. Total sales, par value, $18,550,900. Old United States bonds were unchanged.

The committee organized in Council Chamber with celebrity by electing Councilman Alexander A. Abrahams of the Fifth ward, chairman, and Miss Clara Southwick of the Consumers League, as Secretary. It was the second attempt made by the committee to organize and it was what might be termed in jockey parlance, a running one.

Lincoln, Neb., March 12.—(Special.)—The constitutional convention is getting to that point where the warm sunshine is calling for the members to get back and plant their potato crop and so the great problem now is to keep the members until the job is over.

The well-known Hammond case, recently in the supreme court, entered into the proceedings Friday when Peterson of Lancaster introduced an amendment to 221 of the bill of rights governing the trial by jury. Peterson's amendment extended the proposal for five-sixths agreement to govern by including cases of constructive contempt. Judge Albert of Columbus said that if Mrs. Hammond were to be allowed jury trial her son would not have been returned to her.

The convention passed the following proposals:

Number 227: forbidding public utilities to consolidate stock property or franchise of competing or parallel property without permission of the State Railway Commission. Vote, 76 to 2.

Number 328: referring to mutual and cooperative organizations. Mutual or cooperative organizations may limit number of shares to one stockholder and the right of transfer, and one vote to each stockholder.

Number 350: laws may be enacted, providing for the investigation, submission and determination of controversies between employer and employees in any business affected with the public interest, and for the prevention of unfair business practices and unconscionable gains affecting the public welfare. An industrial commission may be created for the purpose of administering and enforcing such laws, and an appeal shall lie to the supreme court from the final orders and judgment of such commission. Vote, 62 to 9.

Number 327: the reorganization of the executive department. It was passed with the understanding that it will be amended on its next passage through committee of the whole, reinstating the land commissioner and other minor changes. Vote, 7 to 6.

Number 352: providing for the election of railway commissioners by districts and taking away the right of the Railway Commission to regulate publicly owned common carriers or local public utilities. This proposal failed at first to get sufficient votes, but with the understanding that it would be amended, making the commissioners elective at large, when up for third reading it finally passed by vote of 15 to 50.

of the man who seeks their support
for the presidency, certain ideals that
they first are pretty sure he is going
to live up to-


For instance, they are going to
choose man, who by his life and
work has shown himself to be just and
fair to all factions, classes and in
terests, party-free man and a true
American.


The American voter, and particu-
larly the women voters of the coun-
try, are weary to death of machine
politics.


The new women voters of the
country, together with the growing
Independent vote of thinking men.
| believe will be instrumental in elect
ing to office a man who will serve
the people, and who by his wise, lib
eral leadership of our people will
serve the world in these critical
times.


Women voters, perhaps even bet
ter than men, know that we require
radical changes in our government
There have been great changes in the
past few years, and out of this up
heaval, we need man who, as head
OF the government, will point the
way to new ideals and several fun
damental readjustments.


We women know such a man,
man whose work throughout the war
in the stricken countries of Europc
has brought him in touch with every
national and international problem
a man whose business career has Civ
en- him a keen insight into questions
of transportation, finance, produc-
ton and distribution, social and in
dustrial re-adjustment and most of
the important questions that this

The light soils found in Virginia
and the Carolinas are very deficient

Therefore, the problem of supplying
the deficient organic matter is one of

fronted. Humus—the life of the soil—
must be put in the soil for the fol-
lowing reasons.
1. Humus is the chief source of
supply of nitrogen.

2. Humus, when decaying, makes
available plant food from the store of
unavailable plant food in the soil.
3. Humus acts as a sponge and in-
creases the water-holding capacity of
the soil.

4. Humus makes the soil more
mellow and granular.

5. Humus binds together the soil
particles and thus prevents the soil
from drying by wind or washing by
rain.

6. Humus permits air to enter
heavy clay soils more readily.
7. Humus makes soil darker in col-
or.
8. Humus furnishes food for count-
less numbers of bacteria that are
helpful to plant growth.
9. Humus prevents baking.
All organic matter produced on the
farm that cannot be used as food
should be returned to the soil to sup-
ply humus. Corn and cotton stalks,
straw, and all spoiled hay, etc., should
not be burned, for in burning, the or-
ganic matter is destroyed. They
should be worked into the soil where
they will decay and form humus. All
manure produced should be saved
and spread upon the fields, and WORKED
into the soil. If enough material is
not furnished in this manner to kee-
p up the supply of humus then some
crop should be plowed under for this
purpose.
The best crops to plow under for
green manure are cowpeas, soy bean,
sweet clover, and rye. Any of these
crops may be planted in the spring
and plowed under in June in time
to plant a crop of sorghum or corn
in July. In this way seasons are
not lost and the soil is benefited.

ASPARAGUS, our first succulent
green vegetable, is the dainty
aristocrat of the vegetable kingdom and
is so universally liked that many
housewives are keen to conserve such
perishable product by canning; yet
they are very much disappointed when, upon
opening the jars that were so carefully
done, to find the grass that was canned
with such care unfit for food.


"It is sour and mushy," writes one
housewife, while another tells me that
she was so terribly disappointed after
all her trouble and hard work that it
almost made her sick to have to throw out
the twenty-five jars that she canned;


This is just the place to stop and
reason out the trouble. Chemists know
of, and call this trouble thymolphylle,
or sour fat, that is, the product be-
comes acid sour and mushy, but does
not effervesce. Now, so much for the
description of this trouble with which
we are more or less familiar—but what
causes it?


Thymolphylle, or sour fat, is caused
by the fact that the asparagus con-
tains vegetable fluid which very
much resembles milk; that is, a mud
which contains a vegetable casein. It
becomes sour or develops lactic acid
and ferment in a temperature from 90 to
100 degrees Fahr., and, if the as-
paragus is cut and then left to stand in
the sun, or is packed into crates and
then the crates placed closely together
so that the ventilation is poor, or if
the grass is allowed to stand in the
heated storeroom or kitchen, it is also
absolutely a waste of time, energy and ma-
terial to can this grass.


To be absolutely successful, the large
farmers have found that they must can
the grass right in the field where it is
grown; thus it is put into the can and
under the process before the sun is high
in the heavens to dry off the dew. This
method prevents failure.


So, if you have no asparagus patch
of your own, and if you are not able to
buy it from a neighbor who will cut it
for you, be cautious and don't can
asparagus.


Now let us start with the knowledge
that you can either obtain the necessary
supply from your own or from a neigh-
bor's garden. Do not work in the
kitchen if it can be helped; select
shady and cool, breezy porch. Find how
many stalks will fit the number of jars
that can be processed at once.


Now trim the stalks for size and
throw into a large pan of cold water
to free from sand. Then gather a few
stalks in your hand and twirl around
in the water to loosen the sand in the
fins. Place in a piece of checkered
cloth and plunge into a large preserving
kettle of boiling water. Cook for three
minutes and then remove from the kettle

platter and spread out in single layer,
then pack quickly into sterilized jars.

use the old fashioned mason jar, just
screw the lid as far as it will go with-
out pressure, and then give it one-half
turn back to loosen. Place at one
in the hot water bath and process to
three and one quarter hours. It
means that from the minute the water
starts boiling it should boil continu-
ously for three and one quarter hours.

led to a misunderstanding and to a

personal quarrel between Darwin and

himself that was never resolved.

There is an extraordinary record

here of Butler's personal relationships.

He was capable, in spite of his satiric

outlook on human nature, of the most

exotic and idealistic friendships for

men: The record of his friendship for

Pauli, young journalist whom he met

in New Zealand, is a curious one. It

was the friendship of a diffident, shy,

poetical man for a confident, snowy,

worldly man, and it led to a doleful

devotion on the part of Butler. Pauli

thought if he could get to England and

become a barrister he might have some

chance of success, and Butler under-

took to take him back with him and to

finance him until he might earn a com-

petency at the law. Through all the

displeasure of his family, through

very deceit and humiliation that

Pauli himself later put upon him, he

continued him the allowance of $200 a

year until Pauli's death thirty years

later put an end to this strange

friendship, when he found that for

many years Pauli had been earning

five times that amount. For years

Pauli refused to let Butler know

where he lived, and Butler learned of

his death through newspaper notice.

And the tragic truth of this strange

friendship which Butler knew was that

"his white heat of devotion" bored

Pauli.

There is recorded another re-

markable friendship developed when Butler

was fifty-six, and this time for a young

man, Hans Faesch, who seems to have

been in no way a remarkable person.

The small circle of people who made

up Butler's personal attendants and

close friends were riveted to him by

strong bonds of affection which no

trial could break down. He took a

deep delight in people of a racy, ma-

tive, pungent wit; and in his personal

attendants, in his charwoman, his

laundress and his clerk. Alfred Cathie,

he had a rare assortment of charac-

ters. Cathie tyrannized over him and

decided matters of state for him. He

was a person of such swift, original

judgments as Butler loved.

Butler was chary of women, and

regarded them heretically and real-

istically. At the studio where he stud-

ied art for many years the women

students called him the Incarnate

Bachelor. He had a few cautious

friendships with women, but it is plain

that he was desperately afraid of any

romantic attachment. Two threatened

him in the course of his life—the first

for a surprisingly beautiful Italian

peasant girl named Isabella and the

other for Miss Savage. She was a

woman of his own temper of mind:

satiric, skeptical and witty. She was a

cripple, not at all beautiful, but, to

judge from the quite remarkable cor-

respondence, a woman of great humor

and charm. She had an understanding

of his genius and a devotion for him

not unlike his for Pauli, but as he had

bored Pauli, so she bored him.

No one stood so isolated from his

period of lionhood following "Erewhon"

as he met Sir George Trevelyan and John

Morley and was disrespectful of them.

Browning, Tennyson, Meredith and

Rossetti he openly derided. He lived

entirely out of literary and social

circles, and as time went by his def-

iant solitude grew more and more

marked. In the end he was a sort of

Ishmael from all the literary and scien-

tific cliques. So that in 1899, when some-

one wrote requesting his influence,

"I am terribly out of favor with

all of them, the reviewers! I

never write on any subject unless I

believe the opinion of those who have

the ear of the public to be mistaken,

and this involves that every

book I write runs counter to the men

who are in possession of the field;

hence I am always in hot water.

The complete isolation, or worse than

isolation, in which I stand robs me of

all power to do a good turn to any one

else, however much I might wish to

do so."

Many of Butler's intensest causes

seem pedantic quibblings. It is diff-

icult to understand the heat with which

he fought to prove that the Odyssey

was written by a woman, or that Shake-

speare's sonnets were of a certain

period, or his studied indifference to all

musicians but Handel. There are

a dozen instances by which he proved

himself truly descended from Dr.

Butler, the famous pedagogue. But in

the fearlessness with which he sought for

the truth, in the faithfulness with

which he tended his lights, in the

breadth of his vision, he was an impas-

sioned lover of life. Only one valuing

it deeply could have made such fierce

jests about it. And only one tragically

knowing its limitations could have said,

as he did when he was asked to speak

on "How to Make the Best of Life":

"I do not even know how to make the

best of the twenty inmates your com-

mittee has placed at my disposal.

Life is like playing violin solo in

public and learning the instrument as

one goes on. One cannot make the

best of such impossibilities."

NEW YORK, July 20.—Breeding silver foxes in the frozen North for their expensive pelts is a picayune financial proposition compared to the possibilities of breeding and raising monkeys whose glands will be used for the restoration of vitality, according to Dr. Serge Noronoff, Paris surgeon, who has come to the United States to perform gland transplanting operations in colleges and before medical clinics.

He urged that monkey farms be established in the United States on a large scale. He said his operation would increase the life of a man seventy years to more than a century. Several operations performed on Frenchmen have been successful, he declared and at the present time one of his patients is heading an expedition into the French Congo to obtain chimpanzees which will form the nucleus of a farm in France.

LAW PREVENTS OPERATIONS.

The immediate purpose of his trip to the United States is to perform an operation transferring the interstitial glands of a person who had met sudden death in healthy condition to some man lacking in youth. Dr. Noronoff said French laws prohibiting the mutilation of corpses have prevented him from performing this operation before.

"In France I received numerous letters from men offering one or more glands to science, but amounts they asked for this sacrifice were so fabulous it prevented men needing new glands from taking advantage of their offer," said the French surgeon. "In some of the cases I have not cut away the existing glands, but have merely added in them. The results were just as satisfactory as though both had been replaced.

"These glands, when removed from persons who have died a violent death, can be placed on ice and used several hours later with good results. The operation is neither difficult nor dangerous and should prove popular. In the month I am to remain in the United States I am willing to perform this operation without charge wherever cases are provided for me."

HAS RIVAL HERE.

Dr. Noronoff was informed that he had a rival in the theory of gland transplanting in Dr. John H. Brinkley, surgeon of Milford, Kan., who holds to the theory that goat glands should be used instead of monkey glands. Dr. Brinkley recently performed an operation upon a man in New York City which was reported to be successful and he claims to have operated successfully on fifty-four people since December, 1917.

Monkey glands are better than goat glands for several reasons, said Dr. Noronoff. "The blood of monkeys can scarcely be distinguished from that of humans and monkeys are the most highly developed animals, being susceptible to many diseases of man. Also, monkeys are more prolific than goats. Many of my earlier experiments were on goats, but the 50 operations I performed proved conclusively to my mind that monkey glands are the best."

MADAME SONIA SEROVA, the Russian star dancer, is to appear a season with the Japanese Michio Itow, in series of matinees, commencing next FRIDAY at the Selwyn Theater, sponsors a new theatre, which will be inaugurated before the new season commences. This playhouse will be devoted exclusively to the dance and will be conceived with full appreciation of the special demand of dancers, who of late have taken so conspicuous position in the entertainment catalogue of New York metropolis.

It has long been the desire of Madame Serova to establish such playhouse, and her plans bore fruit two years ago. "The thousands of dance lovers in New York are entitled TO witness their favorite art under conditions as favorable as those who choose the drama or music," says Madame Serova, "but, unfortunately, there are no theaters in New York where these dances can be given during the evening, hence we are compelled to resort to matinees. New York has the theaters of every sort, but those seeking to cater to dance devotees are sadly lacking in their qualifications. for grinding meat. In the same way, a
bird that does not use its wings will in a
few millions of ages lose power of
flight. But this principle holds good
only so far. When an animal has become
specialized and adapted to his environ-
ment, so far as his structure will permit
without endangering the balance neces-
sary to existence, it usually stops
changing and finally, it is supposed,
loses power of development.


There is a difference of opinion as to
whether man has reached the point
where he is best adapted to his surround-
ings, or whether he will continue to
evolve. Mr. Gidley says that man's
present mechanical arrangement is per-
manent. He refutes the suggestion that
man's jawbone will shrink and his teeth
drop out because he eats more soft foods
and does not chew so vigorously as his
cave-man ancestors. Man knows enough
about chemistry to understand what kind
of food are necessary to insure health,
and there is little prospect of his jaw
disappearing on a balanced ration.


OUR TOES ARE SAFE


Nor does Mr. Gidley think we need
to worry over the prophecy that our de-
scendants' heads will be all brain—not
by present indications.


We have been further warned by some
men of science that our toes, all except
the big one, are already useless from
lack of exercise, and that eventually they
will grow shorter and disappear altogether,
like the horse's long discarded
toes. This, too, Mr. Gidley regards
as groundless, for while the muscles of
the shorter digits are not particularly
visible in modern shoes, yet we do use
them in balancing. Statues of the old
Greek gods and athletes show that they
pushed themselves on the inside of the
foot, a method which gave both the app-
earance and feeling of lightness. Had
the Greek ideal persisted, the outer toes
of man might by now be almost ab-
sorbed, probably to the improvement of
human posture.


And few scientists insist that it is, in
fact, not the case. So slowly does
nature progress. For instance, it took
the horse a few million years to grow
the hoof which he needed for speed, as the
horse was not built for fighting. He had
to be always poised on the tips of his
four-toed feet ready to escape when an
armored dinosaur or a megatherium came
rumbling on him. If you go into almost
any big museum, you can see the bones
of the horse's foot at different stages of
development. Biologists have ex-
humed the bones of horses that lived
millions of years ago. These horses were
about the size of a dog and had four
toes. Before that it is believed that there
must have been five. Three million years
later, there were only three, and the
middle digit had by that time become
long and resembled a hoof, while the
bones of the toes on each side had short-
ened until they did not reach the ground.


MAN A WEAK ANIMAL


Because he specialized in speed, the
horse can now run as fast as 40 miles an
hour, while man at his swiftest can maxi-
mum only about 20. Man is not a specialized
animal. It has been pointed out to his
confusion that a flea can jump 1000 times
its height, whereas man needs to
go only twice his six feet in proportion to his size. Man has not as much
jumping power and he cannot walk
as fast as a fly. He has not learned to
see in the dark like the cat.


But it is lucky for man that his an-
cestors did not concentrate on beat-
ing the monkeys at tree athletics or the horse
at foot racing. If they had, we should
not to-day be much farther advanced
than the animals we might have
evolved from.


Man's progress is supposed to be due
to his use of his brain, and the fact that
he developed two hands and two feet in
sing of four of one or the other. The best
clues to ancient man so far dis-
covered are part of a skull, a thigh bone,
and two teeth. These were found
in Java, and, judging by the stratum of soil
in which they were lying, geologists de-
clare that the man lived 500,000 years
ago. Pithecanthropus, as the scientist
named the antique Javanese, was a full
developed man, though with rather ap-
pealing features.


The Javanese man of a half million
years ago was one of the animals whose skel-

Millions of years ago in the age of rel-
ics, flourished the armored dino-
saurs which to most people is the symbol
of prehistoric times. But even the dinosaur
is young as the age of the world goes. Dr.
Waicott of the Smithsonian Insti-
tute estimates that animal life started
on the earth 41,000,000 years ago. Some-
where between then and the very recent

It is planned to visit every town and hamlet and in speeches urge the voters to call upon their representatives in the House to support the suffrage resolution. Particular attention will be paid to Sussex and Kent counties, where the opposition is the strongest. It also is planned to obtain petitions and signed statements from as many voters as possible to present to the legislators.

When the Legislature reassembles on Monday after the Easter holidays suffrage advocates said tonight they were confident their strength in both branches would be materially increased. They hoped to obtain reconsideration of the ratification resolution by the House, but should this fail, they pointed out that an identical resolution is still in the Senate, and if passed by the upper branch it could be brought before the House at any time. The suffragists claim to have a majority of one in the Senate.

Friends of equal suffrage were greatly encouraged by the announcement of Alfred I. du Pont that he would support the ratification resolution and do all he could to secure its passage. Governor Townsend said to-day Mr. du Pont's action would greatly strengthen the suffrage cause and might cause a reversal of yesterday's action by the House.

Anti-suffragist leaders felt secure in their victory and declared that, so far as Delaware is concerned, the equal franchise amendment is dead. They said that Mr. du Pont's announcement would have no effect whatever, pointing out that some of the most powerful political influences, both national and state, had already been brought to bear in behalf of the measure without success.

news. Jekyll replied that he had heard
it cried in the street. Utterson said:

and I want to know what I am doing.
Are you hiding this murderer?"

will never more be heard of."

letter to his master. Poole was sure

he said: "The two hands are in many

They decided to break down the

They stood before the door and Ut-

On the table was a confession.

HAPPY NEWS FOR THE SALVATIONISTS

Happy news for the Salvationists is the arrival of Mrs. J. L. Simonson, from Seattle, Wash., who will have charge of the relief work of the Salvation Army in Birmingham. After December 1, Mrs. Simonson's relief station will be open at headquarters in the Lyric building, where she will direct her attention particularly to the needs of the poor.

Although relief has always been a part of the work of the Salvationists of this city, it has been carried on to such an extent by other duties that the relief office has been kept open only in the forenoons. With Mrs. Simonson to superintend the work and give full time to it, the door of her office will never be locked at any hour in the day when a needy call comes. Under her direction the relief department will be recognized and broadened in its activities.

HERE TO COOPERATE

"I am here to co-operate with every organization in the city which ministers to the needs of the poor spiritually or materially," stated Mrs. Simonson yesterday. "I hope I shall be able to be of some service and do some good in Birmingham," she added quietly.

Upon this statement of his wife, Brigadier Simonson's good-natured smile broadened perceptibly when he said, "Good? There is always good wherever she is. I tell you it was good just to see her when I went to the Terminal station the other day to meet her."

"Charity begins at home," was the rejoinder.

"But it doesn't end there," replied Mrs. Simonson, while she explained that during the months she had been stationed in the west she had been anxious to join Brigadier Simonson not only for the sake of helping him in his territorial work in Alabama, Tennessee and Mississippi, but also for the sake of the particular work that will engage her attention in this community.

So it is, that Mrs. Simonson comes to her new home here not only with the title of "Brigadier" that sounds as interesting and official as her husband's, but with warm motherly sympathy for the young and the old who are suffering, and with the equipment of years of experience in relief work, which she has undertaken in every city that has been visited.

Mrs. Simonson's headquarters

LOCAL CONDITIONS

"Until our relief office is opened here on December 1, expect to spend the time in learning something of the situation in Birmingham," Mrs. Simonson stated. "I wish to be in touch, and to cooperate with the church and civic organizations, and the community and social service clubs, that deal with people in need.

"In our work heretofore we have also helped," she informed. "Very often officers have called on us to help them in cases that do not seem to need the police court so much as they need a little friendly counsel or material aid. Sometimes these aids will restore a person's self-respect. Or it may be a little medical attention that is needed, or treatment at the hospital; and sometimes in our work we supply food to those who are actually hungry."

CHARITY THAT CHEERS

"Our purpose is to practice the charity that does not impoverish, but that which cheers, and which helps the discouraged to regain their self-respect," assured Mrs. Simonson.

"In all my experience with this work," she continued, "I have found that the trouble with many needy people is lack of self-respect in a habit or dependence on others. The loss of this is so much more serious than any trouble through poverty or sickness, that our big task is to encourage them back to self-confidence and self-respect."

In illustration of this, Mrs. Simonson said, "I can take you to a clean, prosperous lunch room in one of the cities in which we lived. The history of this lunch room and bakery is the history of the little woman who has charge of it. She and her husband were self-respecting, hard working people, who owned their own home and who were educating a family of children. New York, Nov. with the opening of the polls less than a hours away both Republican and Democratic headquarters today took up the stride which will carry them in the final scene of the presidential contest to-morrow, either to victory or defeat.

Both major parties, began their campaigning day by reasserting confidence in the election of their candidates.

Cox and Roosevelt will win," declared George White, Democratic national committeeman.

Will H. Hays, leader of the Republican forces, translated his expectations into figures, expressing the conviction that Harding will have no less than 395—probably 395—electoral votes out of the possible 531. The number required to elect is 266.

Interest in the last day of the great fight centers in the final desperate attempt to bring over the doubtful states with large electoral votes to deliver, or to save United States senators in other doubtful states, where the electoral vote is not large enough to be indispensable. The salient example of states in the first category is Ohio, home state of the two principal candidates, with 25 votes, while the outstanding case of the second class is Nevada, with only three.

Other states where the eleventh hour contest is intense with both parties sanguine of success are Arizona, Kentucky, Maryland, New Mexico, Tennessee, North Carolina and Oklahoma. All of these, as well as the Buckeye state are claimed by both Republicans and Democrats.

Second only in interest to the outcome of the voting is the subject what will the women do?

Speculation of both major parties disclaim possession of advance information on what is to be expected of the new class of voters exercising their franchise in all the states for the first time.

Speculation in ordinarily well informed political circles, centers about the numerical proportion of women who will vote tomorrow in comparison with the male vote, section distribution of the women's votes, and the probabilities to be looked for. Most of the researchers declare that the recent Maine election, where the women's vote was well under half that of the men, can be considered no criterion for predicting national election results. Women in states where universal suffrage has been obtained some years are expected to outdo their newly enfranchised sisters, and, on the other hand, the experts admit this hypothesis also may be wrong.

The Socialist party has made claim for the largest proportion of the women vote. With the new voters properly belonging to the party added to the non-socialists, who, they say, will vote the ticket again in protest against the imprisonment of the party's presidential nominee Eugene V. Debs, the Socialists predict a vote of at least 500,000. In 1916 the Socialist vote was less than 1,000,000.

If any of the six national parties start out to break electoral college records tomorrow, they must aim at those set up in the election of the ticket headed by President Wilson. In 1912 his majority of 435 was the greatest of the elections.

And morn brings a message
Hidden we'll.

A tint on the wing,
And the bright wind whistles,
And the pulses sting.
Perish dark memories!
There's light ahead;
This worlds for the living,
Not for the dead.
In the shining city,


On the loud pave,
The life-tide is running
Like leaping wave.
How the stream quickens
AS noon draws near!
No room for loiterers,
No time for fear.
Out on the farmlands
Earth smiles as we'll;
Gold-crusted grain fields,
With sweet, warm smell.
Whir of the reaper,


Like giant bee;
Like Titan cricket,


Thrilling with glee.
On mart and meadow,
Pavement and plain;
On azure mountain,


On azure main
Heaven bends in blessing;
Lost is but won;
Goes the good rain cloud
Comes the good sun;
Only babes whimper,
And sick men wall,
And faint hearts and feebl


hearts,


And weaklings fail.
Down the great currents
Let the boats swing;
There never was winter
But brought the spring.


Edward Rowland Sill.

Not for the dead.
In the shining city,

On the loud pave,
The life-tide is running
Like leaping wave.
How the stream quickens
As noon draws near!
No room for loiterers,
No time for fear.
Out on the farmlands
Earth smiles as well;
Gold-crusted grain fields,
With sweet, warm smell.
Whir of the reaper,

Like giant bee;
Like Titan cricket,

Thrilling with glee.
On mart and meadow,
Pavement and plain;
On azure mountain,

On azure main
Heaven bends in blessing;
Lost is but won;
Goes the good rain cloud
Comes the good sun;
Only babes whimper,
And sick men wail,
And faint hearts and feeble

hearts,

And weaklings fail.
Down the great currents
Let the boats swing;
There never was winter
But brought the spring.

Edward Rowland Sill.

Inasmuch as August is the critical month for the crop in the great corn belt of the middle west 1t is uncertain whether the promise of a crop almost equal to the enormous ones of 1912 and 1917 will be fulfilled. Improvement was reported during July in the important corn states with the exception of Illinois and as a result a crop forecast of 224.000,000 bushels larger than that predicted July 1 was issued.

 There was improvement in the potato crop and indications are that the crop will exceed 400 900 900 bushels for the fourth time in the country's history.

 The tobacco crop. which has been promising from the start. has shown additional improvement and probabili- ties are that it will exceed the record crop produced in 1918 by about 200,- 100000 pounds. Total production is forecast at 1.544,000,000 pounds.

JERUSALEM, July 7.—Demanding a complete reorganization in the administration of the Zionist body, to-day demanded the organization of an international Jewish militia for the purpose of defending Palestine. A group of young British Zionist activists went into secret session to-day to draft a platform which they insisted to throw into the teeth of the Zionist conference now sitting.

This action of the young firebrands resulted in the most sensational incident of today. It foreshadows bitter shocks upon the floor of the Zionist conference. The activists are led by Isaac Grossman, a Russian resident in London.

Grossman outlined the most important activist demands as follows:
1. An international militia to guard the Holy Land and to replace the British troops.
2. Instead of "selective," as advocated by convention.
3. The formation of an international Jewish congress outside the Zionist organization; to give the Jews of the world an opportunity of making their wishes heard in the future.
4. The immediate floating of a loan to finance the Jewish settlement in Palestine, asking Jews of the world to contribute 10 per cent of their securities.
5. A drastic reorganization of the reactionary governing boards of the Zionist organization and injection of new blood into executive positions.
6. As there are only 4,000 Jews in Palestine, they are unable to furnish the necessary 10,000 militia troops, so we must organize volunteers in America, England, Russia, and the other countries, said Grossman.

Justice Brandeis and the Elders in the convention declare that an international Jewish army would strengthen the Zionists in diplomatic engagements. Max Nordau also proposes the demand for such an army. However he favors the proposal of unrestricted immigration.

Brandeis, associate Justice of the United States Supreme Court, was elected president of the International Zionist Conference which commenced today, as the first Zionist gathering in seven years, to formulate a political program that will be urged at least. Dr. Nordau, of London, was named honorary president; American and four European delegates were present, as representatives of several civilized countries. Dr. Nahum Sofer, of Bern, as chairman, said the conference must consider the question of immigration and finance.

(Manchester Guardian.)

Any signs of the direction in which the mind of youth is turning are worth noting. At the Cambridge University Union debate on Tuesday night a motion against the adoption of any system of compulsory service was carried by a vote of two to one. Before the war, when Lord Roberts' compulsory service agitation was at its height, such a motion would almost certainly have been defeated by a large majority either at Cambridge or Oxford. It is often thoughtlessly said that the war was a vindication of that agitation. Evidently, in the minds of a typical assembly of educated young Englishmen, most of whom served as officers in the war, it was the opposite. The demonstration should surprise nobody. There never was during the war the same proportion of support for conscription among soldiers serving abroad that there was among civilian politicians in England. The Australian troops, when polled in France, voted against conscription in Australia. At the time when tribunals of elderly civilians at home were battling conscientious and unconscientious objectors alike, sometimes with a show of doing it out of regard for our fellows in the trenches, "our fellows in the trenches" were quite free from any desire to depend for any fraction of their safety upon some pressed man who thought it wicked to fight, or upon one who feared it so much as to go to the trouble of pretending to think it wicked. A great deal—not all, but a great deal—of the support given to conscription at all times has been due to the longing of some people to inflict its hardships upon others. Such support, like the hustling of the Quakers and other recusants during the war, is really penal in spirit, not military. The purely military valuation of conscription has always been less enthusiastic, and its valuation by veterans of the late war is low indeed. Whatever the other arguments in its favor, it brought new dangers into the trench life of professional and volunteer soldiers, and it lowered the military value of any given number of troops and tended to disturb calculations based upon that number. It is eloquent of the drift of informed opinion that in a debate among men of more than average intelligence who have, in the main, been subalterns in the war, conscription should be condemned by a majority of more than two to one. In any other assembly of the kind it would probably have the same fate.

Must We Join the League or Else Prepare to Fight?

Secretary Daniels declares that if we do not join the League of Nations it must build "incomparably the greatest navy in the world."

The Lincoln Star (Ind.) indorses the secretary's view, arguing that the United States must be either for the League or against it. We are, at present, for the League, and logically the task of supplying the anti-league military strength falls upon this country's shoulders.

"Unless the United States is as strong as the League of Nations," the Star argues, it is subservient, in the dry at least, to the League and might as well be a member of the League, even though at the great sacrifice which the obstructionist senators say it would mean to become a party. If the United States is not to become subservient here is but one road open, and that is "an immensely enlarged navy and army."

"If we refuse to take a place in the League," declares the San Antonio Express (Tex.), "all the nations would consider themselves required to go on enlarging their navies, with the result that such rivalry would force the United States either to outdistance all other countries in this respect, or sink to the position of second, third, or perhaps fourth place among the nations of the world." The Portland Oregonian (Ore.) is of the same mind, believing that "by accepting reasonable reservations we can obtain the predominant position in the League" and "escape the necessity for a great navy" but that "if a world beating navy should become necessary, responsibility must be shared by both the Democrat and the Wilson standpatters."

"The country is at peace or at war," the New York World (N.Y.) declares, "there is no third condition. New London, July 26. — The New London physicians are not affiliated with the American Federation of Labor and like organizations; therefore it is just a little bit surprising to learn that some of the local doctors contemplated establishing an "open" hospital, whatever that may mean in medical parlance. It is understood that some of the most reputable physicians in the city for some real or imaginary breach of professional etiquette, ethics or something of that kind, have been penalized to the extent that they are not permitted to treat their patients at the hospital, are not members of the hospital staffs and not entitled to hospital privileges. If that be so it can readily be understood why a physician who was in charge of the naval hospital here, did so much outside practice while in the service, that he decided to locate here after his discharge from the naval service. As he did considerable surgery, and there was no room for him or his patients at the hospital, he opened one of his own.

It may be that some of the doctors are aboard the craft that is not permitted to berth at the hospital, and that may be the reason why they are combining to have what is termed an open hospital, where any reputable doctor could obtain all the advantages of giving patients hospital treatment on an even basis with any other member of the "profession." It is evident that labor language is being adopted by the physicians, for, according to their say—there are "closed" hospitals in New London or will be when the proposed "open" hospital is established here.

The proposed "open" hospital, if the present plans prevail, will be located in Pequot avenue, facing the harbor, a very admirable location, in the large building that was headquarters for Marines during the world war. The structure could readily be converted into a large hospital, with plenty of room for enlargement. There is actual need for material increase of hospital accommodations in New London, "closed" and "open" combined. Even with the proposed additional buildings of the Lawrence Memorial Association, including the immediately needed maternity building, there is still need for another hospital in New London. The open may fill the bill.

The building on Pequot avenue was formerly owned by the late Reuben T. Palmer. He had it moved from the corner of Broad and Hampstead streets to its present location. The moving of that building so inconvenienced public traffic that the ordinance permitting the removal of buildings through the streets was the ultimate result. After its removal, which required two trips, the building having been halved for the purpose, Mr. Palmer had the structure remodeled and generally improved. That building was formerly the home of Henry P. Haven, an old-time whaling merchant, prominent in church and Sunday school work, the founder of the first free evening school in the state, and once a Republican candidate for governor. He was in this house where Miss Frances H. Caulkins wrote much of the History of New London, she being a close relative of the Haven family.

It became necessary for consolidation of the Memorial and Lawrence hospital when the Navy Department took over the Memorial hospital together with the new innhouse, adjacent. This consolidation was carried into effect by legislative consent, and the associated institution is now governed by an interlocking board of directors, to the benefit of both institutions and the general public. The city of New London that donated the land for the Memorial hospital has magnanimously withdrawn all claim against the property, giving the hospital association full power to sell the property and use the proceeds for hospital purposes. This with the cash on hand will be of material aid to the construction of the maternity and other buildings in connection with the original Lawrence hospital.

With characteristic magnanimity the Memorial hospital offers to sell the hospital property in Jefferson avenue to the promoters of the "open" hospital—a ready-made institution ready for almost immediate occupancy. This offer has been made publicly and if there has been response it has not been published. This would indicate that the so-called "closed" hospitals would encourage and welcome the coming of the proposed "open" hospital and regard it as a public necessity, and in no wise as a competitor. All interested in hospital work realize that the present hospital facilities are entirely inadequate. The very first and most important hospital need is the building of that maternity building, and belief exists that the generous public is ready to come across, if need be, in aid of that worthy project. Governor Hebron was misunderstood or probably reported incorrectly on something like that when he was quoted as saying that he had no knowledge of a National Guard company being formed in New London, or elsewhere in the state, and that the company, if such existed, would not receive state recognition. This very week, right here in New London, just such a company was inspected by the adjutant general of the state, passed the required exam, and its officers elected and approved. In due time this same governor, or some other, will give his endorsement of acceptance.

New York, Jan. 9—Announcement was made tonight that, by newly discovered method, coal tar can be made to yield tartaric acid and other important substances which help to lower the costs of living and lessen the blow of prohibition.

The details were explained in a joint paper read before the New York Section of the American Chemical Society at 40 East 41st Street and written by the inventors and patentees of the process, John W. J. Weiss and C. R. Downs, respectively the manager and the chief chemist of a well-known firm of chemical manufacturers of this city.

The basis of the process is method of building up various substances from maleic acid obtained from benzol, one of the derivatives of dark and viscid coal tar. Maleic acid has been separated from the juices of certain plants and fruits, but at so high cost that it could not be put on the market and was considered merely as a laboratory curiosity. By the Weiss-Downs process, benzol is mixed with air and the vapor is passed over a catalyzer, a material which alters the speed of chemical reactions without being in itself affected. On account of their mysterious power to join other substances in chemical wedlock, catalyzers are known as "chemical parsons."

With maleic acid as a base, it is possible to prepare other valuable acids. Of these, the most welcome to the housekeeper and the trade is tartaric, which hitherto has been made from the cream of tartar, solid found in the bottom of wine casks and employed principally in the making of baking powder. The United States before the prohibition wave engulfed the vineyards where wine grapes are raised, produced ten million pounds of tartaric acid. As the cream of tartar cannot be obtained except through the fermentation of the wine, the grape juice industry is able to supply the household want hitherto filled from the waste of the vintner. There was large importation from Europe before the war, but it was checked by the military situation.

During its life, 1909-13, its average ad valorem was under 20 per cent, while the Wilson-Gorman law of Democratic parentage, during its mill-killing career averaged over 8 per cent. The fault lay in the fact that the schedules of the latter were all out of joint. But Senator Curtis's estimate does not entail the adoption of tariffs prohibitively high. Along about 1899, 1900 the average ad valorem just shaded 8 per cent. Assuming that $5,000,000,000 worth of foreign goods can be annually absorbed by this country during the next decade without paralyzing domestic industries, it is plain that a 30 per cent ad valorem would realize $1,500,000,000 in revenue. At the present time, with goods coming in at the rate of $6,000,000,000 annually, about $360,000,000 in customs revenues is the most we can hope for by the end of the current year, this being at the 6 per cent rate.

ual though steady decline in the Gull

nous crop having any large degree of
influence upon keeping up the pro-
ductivity of the soil"

If he has done an average amount of Red Cross reading he will know that small slice out of the other so cents is appropriated to disaster relief.

But unless he is one of the exceptionally few he will not know what disaster relief has meant to the world during the life of the American Red Cross, nor will he realize what small slices of dollars will do if there are enough of them.

In the Northwestern Division, time after time the relief organization has met its crisis and has stood the test. A list of all the Red Cross relief work in times of fire, flood and famine would take pages. Long before the organization under the stress of war and wars results had grown into the lives of millions, disaster relief was one of its foremost activities. The Congressional Charter under which the Red Cross has operated since 1905 sets forth as one of the chief purposes of the organization: to continue and carry on system of relief and to apply the same in mitigating the sufferings caused by pestilence, famine, fires, floods and other great national calamities.

And now, with its wonderful organization of chapters, branches and auxiliaries reaching to the farthermost parts of the nation, its members instructed and ready for action when the occasion arises, Red Cross disaster relief has become accident insurance for the world.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Oct. 8.—Answering President Wilson's White House campaign statement, issued last Sunday, Senator Warren G. Harding, in a speech in this city tonight, ridiculed as a frequently exposed fallacy the argument that Article X of the League of Nations covenant does not usurp the war-making powers of Congress.

The nominee addressed an audience of 10,000 that packed Convention Hall where, on previous occasions, President Wilson and Governor Cox have spoken in defense of the Versailles treaty. Here, in the home city of Senator James A. Reed, the leading Democratic opponent of the league project, Senator Harding declared that if the United States should subscribe to the covenant with Article X in it, American boys conceivably might have to defend Japan's possession of Shantung.

Senator Harding cited the case of Poland to prove his point that only by breach of faith could signatories to the Versailles covenant fail to resist with arms threat against the territorial integrity of member of the league. He declared if we were party to the league he would hate to see America fail as England failed to furnish aid to Poland.

Points Out Fallacy

"In the President's statement," said Senator Harding, "the people are told that the election is to be genuine national referendum and they are to instruct their own government what they wish done. So far as the league is concerned, he says the question which their vote will answer is: Do they wish the Treaty of Versailles ratified, and do they (I quote his exact words) in particular approve of the League of Nations as organized and empowered in that treaty. Those who oppose the treaty in its present form—and there are quite a number of respectable and intelligent people who do oppose it—are charged with gross ignorance and impudent audacity. He tells the people that there is nothing in the covenant which in the least interferes with, or impairs, the right of Congress to declare war, or not to declare war, according to its own independent judgment as the Constitution provides.

"The fallacy of this position has been exposed again and again. Article X, in words of the utmost precision, binds us to an obligation which, under certain easily foreseeable circumstances will require the use of armed forces."

"It is true that the Constitution invests Congress with the sole power to declare war," the Senator continued, "but if war shall become necessary in order to fulfill this or any other treaty provision, Congress must either declare war or repudiate the obligation. This obligation assumed by the signatories to the covenant is absolute and unqualified. Whenever certain specified circumstances arise, no matter how much we might regret it, we would have to keep our promise or sneak out of it. Let no one be deceived—the choice would be between two things: war or dishonor.

"Article X is not only the most dangerous provision in the covenant but, in its sinister possibilities, it is the most dangerous proposition ever presented to the American people."

"America" Drowned in Cheers

The walls and floor of Convention Hall were completely hidden by the great throng that had been waiting there for two hours when Senator Harding appeared at 8 o'clock. The crowd was standing, singing "America," when the features of the Ohioan were framed in a doorway in the north wall of the hall. At once the words of the song were drowned in a roar of cheers. Thousands of tiny American flags were waved.

Senator and Mrs. Harding waved their hands to the crowd. The demonstration continued for about ten minutes, coming to climax with the singing of "The Star-Spangled Banner."

"I am convinced that you love America more than you love the league."

Chicago, April 10.—The railroad
brotherhoods claimed last night they
had won their fight against dissent-
ing members and that the backbone
of the railroad strike had been
broken in Chicago. Leaders of the
radical unions were unwilling to admit defeat. They said while the
brotherhoods had succeeded in win-
ning back few men in Chicago the
strike had swept throughout the
country.

A plea of representatives of the
brotherhoods to railroad mana-
gers for more time to break the
strike was the outstanding feature
of yesterday's developments. The
brotherhoods made their representa-
tions to J. W. Higgins, executive
secretary of the Western Railroad
Managers Association.

According to Higgins the brother-
hoods continue to bring in loyal
men to break the strike.
That the strike was aimed against
the brotherhoods as much as against
the railroads was indicated by
statement of John Grunau, president
of the Chicago Yardmen's Associa-
tion.

"The fight has become one of su-
premacy between the new and the
old unions," he said. "The question
of increased pay has ceased to be
a big factor in the strike.

That the new union was striving
for recognition from the railroads
was shown yesterday when a com-
mittee of dissenters called on the
Railroad Managers Association and
asked it to enter negotiations for
settlement of the strike.

The railroads continue to refuse
to take the leading part in breaking
the strike. They put to work such
union men as the brotherhoods could
supply. No effort was made to
employ non-union workers.

Federal officials approached the
situation with caution. Mediators
made no effort to interfere. It was
indicated they would give the
brotherhoods ample time to bring their men back in line.
